body.p: This article was written as a reflection for a weekly student activity at the Auburn Catholic Student Center called Spirit and Truth. The activity consisted of a short five-to-ten minute speech by a student volunteer, followed by about an hour of praise and worship before the Blessed Sacrament. I have chosen to retain the passages in this article suited for public speaking, lest I need to produce a version of the speech different from what was actually presented.
Tonight I'd like to present a passage from Holy Scripture for us to meditate on; the Words of Institution from the Holy Gospel of St. Matthew, chapter 26:

26 Now as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed, and broke it, and give it to the disciples and said, "Take, eat; this is my body." 27 And He took a chalice, and when He had given thanks He gave it to them, saying "Drink of it, all of you; for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins"

We frequently hear this passage from the mouth of the celebrant in persona Christi at every Mass; yet, we cannot take for granted how important, how miraculous the event on the altar is; especially me, seeing as the Eucharist was the driving force for me to jump ship from 'nondenominationalism' to the one, holy, Catholic, and apostolic Church. So, inspired by the words of St. Thomas Aquinas, I would like to explore the threefold 'past-present-future' nature of the Eucharist. A love letter, if you will, to Christ in the Most Blessed Sacrament.

In pointing to the past, the Eucharist functions as a, hear me out, symbol. While this is not an easy idea to explain to those with a completely symbolic view of communion, Catholics do hold that there must be some symbolism around the Eucharist; however, it cannot be just a symbol. Consider this: do you receive "more Jesus" when you receive both the Most Precious Body and Most Precious Blood? No! They are both fully Christ; so, then, what is the significance of the Eucharist appearing under two forms, or, more formally, two Species? Why must the celebrant consume Christ in both Species for the Sacrifice of the Mass to be valid? Because the symbolism of the Sacrament is not complete until you partake of both Christ's Body and Blood. We know the Elements themselves are not symbolic, far from it, actually, but the symbolism arises out of the true, Real Presence, and is most clearly seen when both Species are received together.

Unfortunately, and for reasons too complex to explain in the moment, many Christians today draw the line at symbolism, but, as I mentioned, we as Catholics also believe the Eucharist is a sacrifice, or, rather, the Sacrifice. A common, albeit misguided, idea of our time is that a biblical sacrifice starts and ends when something of value is lost to atone for some value deficit, say a quality harvest or healthy livestock in exchange for certain sins. This is an incomplete view. Sacrifice, like many things, is only effectatious for you when you are involved or bound to the sacrifice in some way. Throughout Holy Scripture, eating seems to be the most common way people attach themselves to their sacrifices. Under the Abrahamic covenant, priests were commanded to eat a portion of every offering made, while the presenting family were often given the rest of the sacrifice for them to eat. This system is seen in its fullness on Passover; during which, right before His Sacrifice, the New Adam gave us His Most Precious Body and Blood for, quote, "the forgiveness of sins". Following that meal, Christ's Passion began, and as the Paschal Lamb, He was sacrificed once for all; and seeing as His Sacrifice is sufficient for all sin, we as the Church are left only with the need to enter into His Sacrifice. This is why the Mass is a Sacrifice: a bloodless, infinite Sacrifice; fulfilling the need for violent and insufficient sacrifices ad infinitum. A pure and holy Sacrifice in which the carnal and the divine meet. A loving Sacrifice that cleans us with powerful sanctification. The Mass does not crucify our Savior again (God forbid, as that would mean that Calvary was not enough) but presents for us His single Sacrifice, beyond time and space, and through that one Sacrifice, the opportunity for us renew and strengthen our communion with God.

Finally, the future-facing nature of the Eucharist is the promise of the hope to come. As Christians in a fallen world, we easily drift towards one of two extremes: a lust for the natural world, killing all of us but our flesh, or a hatred for the natural world, pushing us towards the radical heresy of Gnosticism. We often loose sight of the true Biblical promise of a new heaven and a new earth! Seriously consider just how significant that is. This promise of a bodily resurrection at the end of time, culminating in the New Eden, where heaven and earth meet, is inseparably tied to the Eucharist. Why? Because Christ said so! See John 6:

53 So Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you have no life in you (I); 54 He who eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day (II). 55 For My flesh is food indeed, and My blood is drink indeed. 56 He who eats My flesh and drinks My blood abides in Me, and I in him (III). 57 As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so He who eats Me will live because of Me (IV). 58 This is the bread which came down from heaven, not such as the fathers ate and died; he who eats this bread will live forever. (V)

Besides the fact this passage lays claim to so many significant Christian dogmas, Christ describes five times, in detail, exactly how the Eucharist brings about our eternal life. One can imagine that, were He to use a modern cliche, Jesus may have said "you are what you eat". For when you eat of Christ's body, you are joined with Him. Look at it this way. At every Mass, a miracle occurs where the natural and supernatural are intertwined so thoroughly that, at its deepest nature, the bread ceases to be and becomes the Body of Christ. This moment, in a poetic way typical of the Holy Spirit, mirrors many of the mysteries of Christ's life, but most notably, Jesus's Incarnation and Resurrection. And just as Consecration ties back to the Incarnation, our reception of Holy Communion connects us to our resurrection.

And this is how the Eucharist is threefold. The past, present, and future, all contained in a small unleavened wafer. It is the Gift of gifts because it contains, no, is the Lord of lords. To eat of the flesh of our Lord is feed our spirit and our body on the food of the Resurrection, to partake of His Passion, to remember His broken body and spilled blood. Here, the perfect Love of our Savior meets our fickle, wavering, imperfect love, and sustains us. For His flesh is food indeed. And for this reason the Eucharist is the source and the summit of Christian faith.
During worship, as we adore Christ together, reflect on this threefold nature of symbolism, sacrifice, and promise. I would like to close in the prayer from the Chaplet of the Most Blessed Sacrament.

My Jesus, I believe that you are truly present in the Most Holy Sacrament. I love you above all things. I desire to receive you into my soul. Since I cannot now receive you Sacramentally, come, at least, spiritually into my heart. I embrace you, and I unite myself entirely to you, as if you had already come; do not permit me to be ever separated from you. Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament, have mercy on us.
